fixes.explanation: Paul doesn't see it that way at all. He says he's “…in no way inferior…” to those super-apostles. Far behind would be the opposite of what he says. He holds his head up here, and I think that's a good place to hold it.

Close, but Paul doesn't name Adam here. He says, “…just as Eve was deceived by the serpent’s cunning…” Adam is Eve's husband, and he's in the garden story too (Genesis 3:6). But in this verse Paul picks Eve to make his point about minds being led astray.

Abel, Adam and Eve's son (Genesis 4:2), comes along after the garden, so he isn't the one Paul reaches back to. Paul says, “…just as Eve was deceived by the serpent’s cunning…” The serpent talked with Eve in the garden (Genesis 3:1–5). Poor Abel wasn't even born yet, friend, he missed that whole conversation.

That's what Paul says. If someone proclaims another Jesus, a different spirit or a different gospel, “…you put up with it very easily.” Notice he says easily, friend. I think that word is what worries him.
If only, friend. Paul says the opposite: “…you put up with it very easily.” Nothing there says anyone gets sent away. He describes a church that puts up with it.
Paul doesn't mention any arguing. He says they “…put up with it very easily.” Easily is the word he picked, friend. I think a few days of arguing would have comforted him a little.

That's it. Paul asks if it was a sin “…because I preached the gospel of God to you free of charge?” He calls that humbling himself so he could exalt them. Think about that question, friend. He's asking whether it was a sin to charge nothing.
The verse says nothing about leaders. Paul says he “…preached the gospel of God to you free of charge?” What he did was cost the Corinthians nothing.

True. Paul asks, “Why? Because I do not love you?” and then he answers right away: “God knows I do!” He calls on God as the One who knows his heart. He asks it and answers it in the same breath, friend.

That's what he says. He'll keep on, “…in order to undercut those who want an opportunity to be regarded as our equals in the things of which they boast.” So his free-of-charge preaching has a purpose. It's aimed at those men's opportunity to be regarded as equals.
Nothing in the passage says they're weary. Paul's word is “false”: “…false apostles, deceitful workers, masquerading as apostles of Christ.” Tired has nothing to do with it.

Pharaoh, the king of Egypt (Exodus 6:11), isn't who Paul names. His words are, “…Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light.” Paul is writing about disguises, and Pharaoh doesn't show up in this passage.

Jezebel, King Ahab's wife (1 Kings 16:31), is a name from the Old Testament, but Paul doesn't bring her up here. He says, “…Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light.” The one wearing the disguise is Satan, and Paul adds that it isn't surprising if his servants masquerade as servants of righteousness (verse 15).
